722.title: Seclusion on the mountain
722.hook: he retreats to Hira for days, taking provisions, praying in the way of Ibrahim (Bukhari)
722.howItsDone: Muslims keep i'tikaf, a retreat for worship in the mosque, especially in the last ten days of Ramadan, following the Prophet's ﷺ practice recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the black stone lifted together: clean money, a wall left short, and a cloak with room for every clan. Your line was: everyone a corner. Who got a real piece of the work? Day seven hundred twenty-two.

A bag of food, packed at home. That's where today's story begins, with something very ordinary. A man fills a bag with provisions, says goodbye to his wife, and walks out of the city and up a mountain. He stays up there for nights at a time. When the food runs out, he comes home, and she packs the bag again. A new part of the sirah opens here, the revelation. And it opens with a packed lunch. Today's word: tahannuth.
screen: `A BAG OF FOOD, PACKED AT HOME.` → `UP THE MOUNTAIN FOR NIGHTS.` → `HOME, AND BACK AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The hadith is in Sahih al-Bukhari, told by 'Aishah. Before revelation, she says, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ began to see dreams that came true like the break of dawn. Then solitude was made dear to him. He went to the cave of Hira and did tahannuth there, and a gloss inside the hadith explains the word: worship, for a number of nights, before he returned to his family. He took provisions for the stay, then came back to Khadijah, and she gave him provisions for the same again. There are two halves to that. Alone on the mountain. And a household at the bottom of it. The seclusion wasn't an escape from Khadijah; she was the one keeping it going, bag after bag. Now the word. Ibn Hisham, who edited Ibn Ishaq's biography, adds a note: the Arabs said tahannuth and tahannuf alike, meaning the hanifiyyah, the way of the hanif. That's the word from day seven hundred two, the hanifs, who turned from the idols toward the God of Ibrahim. So some readers hear in his retreat the old way of Ibrahim, kept by a few seekers, before anything new had been said. What did he pray? The sources don't say. They give us where, and how long, and the food. And the habit stayed. Sahih al-Bukhari records that later, every Ramadan, he spent the last ten days in the mosque in i'tikaf, a retreat for worship, until the end of his life. I'tikaf is still kept in mosques today. Alone with the one.
screen: `SOLITUDE MADE DEAR TO HIM.` · `PROVISIONS FROM KHADIJAH.` · `THE WAY OF THE HANIF.` · `I'TIKAF, EVERY RAMADAN.` · then, large: `ALONE WITH THE ONE.`

segments.voice: The practice: plan a short retreat. Not today, necessarily. Just plan it. Settle, and breathe. Where could you be alone for an hour, or an evening? A park bench, a back room, a walk with no phone. When? Put a day on it. And who's your Khadijah, the person who'd keep things running while you go? You might need to ask them. If you pray, picture yourself praying there. If not, picture the quiet. Let the plan get specific. The bell holds the time.
Tahannuth. Worship in seclusion, night after night, as he did in the cave of Hira, carried by provisions from home. Today's word.
Your line: alone with the one. Today, put your short retreat on the calendar, and thank whoever will hold things together while you're gone. Day seven hundred twenty-two.

723.title: A night in Ramadan
723.hook: at forty, in Ramadan, the angel comes (97:1; 2:185)
723.howItsDone: Muslims seek Laylat al-Qadr in the last ten nights of Ramadan, especially the odd ones, staying up in prayer, recitation and supplication, and some spend those nights in i'tikaf in the mosque.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was tahannuth: worship in seclusion on the mountain, with provisions packed by Khadijah. Your line was: alone with the one. Did your short retreat get a day on the calendar? Day seven hundred twenty-three.

One night on that mountain is different from all the others he spent there. The Qur'an doesn't give its date. It gives its month, and its name, and says it is better than a thousand months. The Prophet told his companions to look for it near the end of Ramadan, and the looking goes on: people stay awake through those last nights, praying and reading, not sure which night it is. Today: a night in Ramadan.
screen: `ONE NIGHT UNLIKE THE OTHERS.` → `A MONTH AND A NAME, NO DATE.` → `STILL WATCHED FOR.`

segments.voice: Start with the month. The Qur'an names it in surah two. Pickthall's translation: "The month of Ramadan in which was revealed the Qur'an, a guidance for mankind." That's why the fast is in Ramadan: it's the month the book arrived. Then the night. A short surah, the ninety-seventh, opens: "Lo! We revealed it on the Night of Power." And it says: "The Night of Power is better than a thousand months." It goes on to say that the angels and the Spirit come down that night, and that it is peace until dawn. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari says the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was forty when revelation began. A man of forty, then, in a cave in the dark, on a night that would get its own surah. What exactly came down that night? Scholars answer in more than one way. Some, following a report from Ibn 'Abbas, say the whole Qur'an was sent down that night to the nearest heaven, then revealed to the Prophet piece by piece over the years. Others focus on this night as the beginning, when the first verses came to him in the cave. Either way, the text is clear about the night and silent about its date. In Sahih al-Bukhari, he tells his companions to seek it in the odd nights of the last ten of Ramadan. So the night is a search. In Muslim teaching the Night of Power comes round again every Ramadan, and so the night it came is sought each year.
screen: `THE MONTH THE BOOK ARRIVED.` · `BETTER THAN A THOUSAND MONTHS.` · `WHAT CAME DOWN THAT NIGHT.` · `SEEK IT IN THE ODD NIGHTS.` · then, large: `THE NIGHT IT CAME.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray one night prayer this week. Settle, and breathe. Pick a night. Not now, this week. Set an alarm a little before dawn, or stay up a little past your usual time. If you pray, there is a night prayer called tahajjud, and you can plan to pray even two short units of it. If you don't pray, plan to sit for a few minutes in the dark, awake, while the house sleeps, and listen. For now, imagine that hour. The quiet. The dark outside. The bell holds the time.
A night in Ramadan. The night the Qur'an says it was revealed, the Night of Power, better than a thousand months, its date kept hidden. Today's word.
Your line: the night it came. Tonight, before you sleep, choose the night this week you'll get up, and set the alarm. Day seven hundred twenty-three.

724.title: Three times, "read"
724.hook: the angel presses him and says read, three times, and then the first five verses (96:1–5; Bukhari)
724.howItsDone: Muslims memorize and learn the Qur'an by repetition, reciting a passage aloud to a teacher again and again until it is held by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a night in Ramadan: the Night of Power, better than a thousand months, its date kept hidden. Your line was: the night it came. Is your alarm set for a night this week? Day seven hundred twenty-four.

Read. I am not a reader. That exchange happens once in the cave, and then again, and then a third time. In between, the hadith says, the angel takes hold of him and presses him until he can hardly bear it. It's a strange, rough beginning: not a vision of light, but a grip, and a word repeated, and a man saying he can't. Today's word is about the repeating: three times.
screen: `READ. I AM NOT A READER.` → `PRESSED, AND RELEASED.` → `THREE TIMES.`

segments.voice: The account is in Sahih al-Bukhari, told by 'Aishah. The angel came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in the cave and said: read. He answered, in Arabic, ma ana bi-qari'. The wording reads most naturally as a denial: I am not one who reads, I can't. Some scholars, pointing to other narrations worded differently, also hear a question: what shall I read? Then the angel took hold of him and pressed him hard, released him, and said again: read. The same answer. A second pressing. Read. The same answer. A third pressing. And then the angel didn't ask. He recited. In Pickthall's words: "Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth, Createth man from a clot." And a few lines on: "Teacheth man that which he knew not." The order matters. The command doesn't come with the ability attached. He says he can't, three times, and the words come anyway, recited to him. Then he carries them home, his heart trembling, the hadith says. Qur'an lessons still have something of that night's shape: a line heard, said back, heard again, until it stays. And there's a hadith that speaks straight to anyone who finds it hard. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet says the one who is skilled in the Qur'an will be with the noble, honored scribes, and the one who recites it with difficulty, struggling over it, gets a double reward. The struggle counts. Read, and read again.
screen: `MA ANA BI-QARI'.` · `PRESSED, THEN ASKED AGAIN.` · `THE WORDS COME ANYWAY.` · `A DOUBLE REWARD FOR STRUGGLING.` · then, large: `READ, AND READ AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The practice: read something difficult three times. Choose one short passage that's hard for you. A verse, a poem, a paragraph from a book you've been putting off. Read it once, slowly, without trying to understand it all. Breathe. Read it again, and notice one word that catches. Breathe. Read it a third time, and let it stay. If you pray, you can read a verse of the Qur'an, even the line from today: read, in the name of thy Lord. Then sit with what's left. The bell holds the time.
Three times. The angel said read, and the Prophet said I am not a reader, three times, before the first verses of surah ninety-six were given to him. Today's word.
Your line: read, and read again. Today, when something is hard to take in, a page, a message, a verse, go back to it one more time before you give up. Day seven hundred twenty-four.

725.title: Khadijah's comfort
725.hook: she tells him Allah would never disgrace him: you keep ties, help the weak, honor guests (Bukhari)
725.howItsDone: Muslims retell Khadijah's words when speaking of good character and of keeping family ties, silat al-rahim, which the Qur'an and hadith treat as a duty and a mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was three times: read, I am not a reader, and then the words given anyway. Your line was: read, and read again. What did you go back to a second time? Day seven hundred twenty-five.

He comes down the mountain shaking. The hadith says his heart was trembling, and that he went straight to Khadijah and said: cover me, cover me. She wrapped him until the fear left. Then he told her everything, and said he feared for himself. What she said next isn't a sermon, and it isn't an explanation. It's a list, and every item on it is something he did. Today: Khadijah's comfort.
screen: `DOWN THE MOUNTAIN, SHAKING.` → `COVER ME.` → `SHE ANSWERS WITH A LIST.`

segments.voice: Here's the answer, as Sahih al-Bukhari keeps it from 'Aishah. Never, by Allah. Allah would never disgrace you. And then her reasons. You keep the ties of kinship. You carry the burden of the weak. You give to those who have nothing. You honor your guest. And you stand by people when real trouble comes. It's an odd kind of comfort. She doesn't explain the angel; she can't, and doesn't pretend to. She argues from evidence she has seen with her own eyes: how he treats people. Her logic: a God who sees all that will not shame this man. Now the first item. The Arabic says he keeps the rahim, a word for the womb, used for the bonds of family. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says the rahim is a branch of ar-Rahman, the Merciful, and that whoever keeps it connected, Allah keeps connected. So the first thing she names is tied, in his own later words, to mercy. Then there's an echo. Years later, when the Prophet's friend Abu Bakr was leaving Mecca under pressure, a chief named Ibn al-Daghinah stopped him and said a man like you should not be driven out, and gave almost the same list. Keeps ties. Carries the weak. Gives to those with nothing. Honors guests. Bukhari records both. The qualities Khadijah named weren't only a wife's praise; an outsider named them too. Allah would never disgrace you.
screen: `NEVER, BY ALLAH.` · `HER REASONS ARE HIS DEEDS.` · `THE RAHIM, A BRANCH OF MERCY.` · `THE SAME LIST FOR ABU BAKR.` · then, large: `ALLAH WOULD NEVER DISGRACE YOU.`

segments.voice: The practice: tell someone the good they do. Settle, and breathe. Think of a person who's frightened, or doubting themselves, or just tired. Then do what Khadijah did: don't argue with the fear, list the evidence. What do they actually do? Who do they show up for? Who do they feed, carry, call, welcome? Make the list specific, three or four things. If you pray, you can thank Allah for the good in them. If not, simply hold the list. You'll use it today. The bell holds the time.
Khadijah's comfort. When he came home afraid, she told him Allah would never disgrace him, and named the good he did: ties kept, the weak carried, guests honored. Today's word.
Your line: allah would never disgrace you. Today, send that person your list, the specific good you've seen them do, with no advice attached. Day seven hundred twenty-five.

726.title: Waraqa's warning
726.hook: Waraqa says the same angel came to Musa, and that his people would drive him out (Bukhari)
726.howItsDone: Muslims remember Waraqa ibn Nawfal with respect as the learned cousin of Khadijah who recognized the revelation, and his warning is retold when the beginning of the Prophet's ﷺ mission is taught.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Khadijah's comfort: she didn't explain the angel; she listed the good he did. Your line was: allah would never disgrace you. Who got your list? Day seven hundred twenty-six.

Good news and bad news, from the same old man, in the same breath. Khadijah has brought her husband to her cousin, Waraqa ibn Nawfal, a learned man, old by now and blind. He listens to the whole account of the cave. Then he tells the Prophet two things. The first is a recognition. The second is a warning, and it's the one the Prophet doesn't expect. Today: Waraqa's warning.
screen: `AN OLD, BLIND COUSIN LISTENS.` → `FIRST, A RECOGNITION.` → `THEN, A WARNING.`

segments.voice: The account is in Sahih al-Bukhari, told by 'Aishah. She says Waraqa had become a Christian before Islam, and that he wrote, and had copied from the Gospel as much as Allah willed. First he says: this is the Namus, the one Allah sent down to Musa. It is understood as the angel Jibril. Then the warning. Waraqa says: I wish I were young. I wish I could be alive when your people drive you out. And the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ asks, in the Arabic, a-wa mukhrijiyya hum? Will they really drive me out? You can hear the surprise. This is the man Mecca called al-Amin, the trustworthy, the one the clans chose to settle the stone. Why would they drive him out? Waraqa's answer is plain: no man has ever come with anything like what you've brought without being treated as an enemy. And if your day reaches me, I will help you with all my strength. He doesn't soften the truth, and he puts himself beside it: if I'm there, I'm with you. That's a hard truth told kindly. The warning did come true. The Qur'an, years later, speaks of the time when those who disbelieved drove him out, and of Allah's help to him in the cave. But Waraqa didn't see it. The hadith ends: not long after, Waraqa died, and the revelation paused. They will drive you out.
screen: `THIS IS THE NAMUS OF MUSA.` · `WILL THEY REALLY DRIVE ME OUT?` · `NO ONE BROUGHT THIS UNOPPOSED.` · `IF I LIVE, I'M WITH YOU.` · then, large: `THEY WILL DRIVE YOU OUT.`

segments.voice: The practice: accept a hard truth kindly. Settle, and breathe. Think of something true that you've been told and haven't wanted to hear. About your health, your work, a relationship, a habit. Notice your first reaction, your own 'will they really?' Let it be there. Then think about who told you, and whether, like Waraqa, they were standing beside you when they said it. If you pray, you can ask for the strength to take it in. If not, just let the truth sit next to you without arguing with it. The bell holds the time.
Waraqa's warning. Khadijah's old cousin recognized the angel who came to Musa, and told the Prophet his own people would drive him out, and promised to stand with him. Today's word.
Your line: they will drive you out. Today, if someone tells you a hard truth, thank them before you answer. Or, if you must tell one, say where you'll stand. Day seven hundred twenty-six.

727.title: The pause
727.hook: revelation pauses, and he grieves, until Ad-Duha and al-Muddaththir come
727.howItsDone: Muslims recite surah ad-Duha (93) in prayer and outside it, and some turn to it in hard or uncertain seasons; the pause in revelation is retold in sirah study alongside the first verses at Hira.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Waraqa's warning. Your line was: they will drive you out. Was there a hard truth you let someone tell you, and did you take it kindly? Day seven hundred twenty-seven.

After the cave, after the command to read, after Khadijah's comfort and Waraqa's warning, a person might expect the next message to arrive the following night. It doesn't. Sahih al-Bukhari ends its account of the first revelation with a short, plain sentence: then the revelation paused for a while. No new verses. No angel at the cave. Just ordinary days in Mecca, and a man waiting for something he cannot summon. The Arabic word for that gap is today's word.
screen: `THE CAVE, THE WORD, THE COMFORT.` → `THEN NOTHING.` → `A MAN WAITING.`

segments.voice: The word is fatrah: a slackening, a lull, a pause. Al-Bukhari's narrations say the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, was saddened by it. The sources don't give it a fixed length, and later writers disagree about how long it lasted, so this lesson leaves the number out. What the reports keep is the feeling and the ending. And readers tell the ending in two ways. In one, from Jabir in al-Bukhari, he is walking when he hears a voice, looks up, and sees the same angel from Hira, seated between the sky and the earth. He hurries home, shaking, and asks to be wrapped up. Then come the opening verses of surah seventy-four, al-Muddaththir, the one wrapped in a cloak. In Pickthall's translation: "O thou enveloped in thy cloak, Arise and warn!" The pause ends with a job. Another report, from Jundub in al-Bukhari, is one some readers link to the pause. The Prophet is unwell and doesn't rise for prayer at night, and someone mocks him, saying that whatever used to come to him has abandoned him. Then surah ninety-three comes, ad-Duha, the morning brightness. Pickthall renders its third verse: "Thy Lord hath not forsaken thee nor doth He hate thee." It answers the mockery almost word for word. And the two endings share something. The silence is not explained away. Nobody in the reports says it was nothing. It is named, it is felt, and then it ends. Some Muslims turn to ad-Duha in hard seasons, and its next verse promises that what comes later will be better than what came before.
screen: `FATRAH: A LULL, A PAUSE.` · `THE ANGEL BETWEEN SKY AND EARTH.` · `ARISE AND WARN.` · `NOT FORSAKEN.` · then, large: `THY LORD HATH NOT FORSAKEN THEE.`

segments.voice: The practice: wait patiently for an answer. Bring to mind one question you've been holding that hasn't been answered yet. A decision, a letter, a prayer, a person. Don't try to solve it now. Just set it in front of you, and breathe beside it. Let the waiting be what it is for two minutes, without filling it. If you pray, you can recite ad-Duha, or simply hold its line about not being forsaken. If you don't, let the bell keep you company in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Fatrah. The pause in revelation after the first verses at Hira, ended by the cloak verses and the morning brightness. Today's word.
Your line: the silence ended. Today, when an answer is slow, give it one more patient breath before you fill the gap. Day seven hundred twenty-seven.

728.title: The first to believe
728.hook: Khadijah first, then Ali, Zayd and Abu Bakr
728.howItsDone: In sirah study, Muslims learn the names of the earliest believers, beginning with Khadijah, and remember them with honor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, fatrah, the pause. Your line was: the silence ended. What did you wait on patiently, and did the gap stay open long enough? Day seven hundred twenty-eight.

Arise and warn, the verse said. Yet the first believers weren't found in a crowd. Not in the marketplace. Not among the chiefs of Quraysh by the Ka'ba. They were the people who shared his meals: a wife, a young cousin, a freed man who lived under the same roof. And one friend from outside the house, a merchant he had known for years. The message began at home. Today: the first to believe.
screen: `ARISE AND WARN.` → `NOT THE MARKETPLACE.` → `THE PEOPLE AT HIS TABLE.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq, the early biographer, gives the order as the sirah tradition remembers it. Khadijah first. Before anyone else, the woman who had heard the whole story that first night, trembling, believed what he told her. Then Ali, his young cousin, who had grown up in that house. Ibn Ishaq tells a scene of Ali coming upon the Prophet and Khadijah praying together and asking what it was. Then Zayd ibn Harithah, the freed man who had chosen to stay with this family rather than go home. Then Abu Bakr, a merchant friend from outside the household. Sources differ about who came first among the men, and some later scholars settle it gently, giving each a place: the first woman, the first youth, the first freed man, the first free man. That gentleness is worth noticing. Nobody had to lose so someone else could win. Now look at who these people are. A wife, a cousin raised as a son, a former slave, an old friend. Not one of them needed a miracle from a stranger. They knew him. They had watched him keep his word, and seen him settle the quarrel over the black stone so every clan held an edge of the cloak. When he said something had happened in the cave, they weighed it against years of what he was. In surah nine, verse one hundred, the Qur'an speaks of as-sabiqun al-awwalun, the first forerunners among the emigrants and the helpers, and says Allah is well pleased with them. Commentators differ over exactly whom the verse means, and some sirah teachers borrow its phrase for these earliest names. Belief, in this story, starts close to home, in the people who had seen the most of an ordinary life.
screen: `KHADIJAH, BEFORE ANYONE.` · `ALI, ZAYD, ABU BAKR.` · `EACH GIVEN A PLACE.` · `THEY KNEW HIM.` · then, large: `THE FIRST FORERUNNERS.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank the first person who believed in you. Settle and breathe. Go back to some beginning: a new job, a first song, a hard year, an idea nobody else liked. Who said yes first? A parent, a teacher, a friend, a stranger who said keep going. Don't stop at the name. Recall the exact words they used, or the small thing they did, as closely as you can. Those are what you'll thank them for. Shape one sentence around it, to send today, or to say in your heart if they're gone. If you pray, you can ask good for them. The bell holds the time.
The first to believe. Khadijah, then Ali, Zayd and Abu Bakr: the people closest to him, who had seen his life before the cave. Today's word.
Your line: first to believe. Today, send one thank-you to someone who believed in you first. Day seven hundred twenty-eight.
